title: On Piano Tuning.
text:
Press any C on a piano, then count the keys before you reach the next one. Twelve notes: seven white keys, five black. I’ve played this layout for decades, and only recently did it strike me as strange. Why twelve? Why not ten, fifteen or even fifty-three (wink)?
The easy answer is convenience. A few more notes per octave would add around twenty keys (the horror). But convenience explains why we don’t have fifty-three notes per octave; but not why don’t we do ten, or seven, which would be even easier. And tuning systems with 19, 24, even 31 notes per octave exist, just glance at Wikipedia [1] on this topic. So, again: why twelve?
My suspicion is that the magic number comes from something deeper: hidden within the arithmetic of musical intervals. This article document my journey of discovering this truth. Beware: there will be mathematics.

title: On Piano Tuning.
text:
The Physics of Pitches
We must first start by introducing the fundamental unit of music - a note. Physically, a note is just air pressure wobbling back and forth. What sets apart notes are its pitches, measured in frequency.






NoteWhat are frequencies?





Frequency is how many times something repeats each second. A vibrating string swings back and forth, and one full back-and-forth is a cycle. The number of cycles per second is measured in hertz (Hz). A 3 Hz wave completes 3 cycles every second, and a 6 Hz wave completes 6, so it repeats twice as fast.





Two waves over one second. The lower one has twice the frequency.




For sound, frequency is pitch: more cycles per second sounds higher. The A string’s 110 Hz means it swings back and forth 110 times every second.



But a note is never one frequency. If you pluck the open A string on a guitar, a tuner will tell you it’s 110 Hz. But run the same sound through a spectrum analyzer, and odds are you will be surprised. It turns out that there are multiple frequencies in a note, not just 110 Hz, but 220, 330 Hz, and so on. The lowest of these, 110 Hz, is the fundamental, and it sets the pitch you hear. The rest, at whole-number multiples of it, are the harmonics, or overtones.
Here is a recording of an open A string, plucked three times. Its fundamental \(f_0\) is 110 Hz, so we expect energy at \(f_0, 2f_0, 3f_0, 4f_0, \ldots\), or at 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz and so on respectively.



                
                    
                    Your browser does not support the audio element.
                
              


A spectrogram shows which frequencies are present at each moment, and brighter indicates higher energy. The dashed lines mark where the theoretical harmonics should be:





Spectrogram of the recorded A string. Dashed lines mark the fundamental \(f_0\) and harmonics \(f_n = n f_0\).




Two things stand out:

The bands sit on the dashed lines. Energy is concentrated at whole-number multiples of 110 Hz, just as predicted.






NoteReal strings are not perfectly elastic!





Real harmonics roughly follow \(f_n \approx n \cdot f_0 \cdot \sqrt{1 + B n^2}\), where \(B\) is the inharmonicity coefficient. Dashed lines may not be perfectly alligned with the peaks.



Higher harmonics are weaker and shorter-lived. Most of the energy sits below about 1000 Hz, and the upper bands fade within a second or so while the low ones ring on.

For why harmonics exist, see my writing on the physics of harmonics in On Harmonics.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Pluck the open A string on a guitar, and a tuner will tell you it’s 110 Hz, meaning the string swings up and down 110 times every second. This count is called the frequency.
But run the same sound through a spectrum analyzer, a tool that splits a sound into its separate frequencies, and it turns out that a single note contains several frequencies at once: not just 110 Hz, but 220, 330 Hz, and so on.
Here is a recording of an open A string, plucked three times. Its fundamental \(f_1\) is 110 Hz, so we expect energy at \(f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, 4f_1, \ldots\), or at 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz and so on respectively.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Shaking a rope
Tie one end of a rope to a post and shake the other end. Shake slowly and the whole rope swings as one big loop. Shake twice as fast and it snaps into two loops, with a point in the middle that stays still. Three times as fast gives three loops. Shake at any rhythm in between and you don’t get a clean pattern at all; the rope just flails.
A guitar string behaves the same way, except both ends are fixed instead of one being in your hand. It has a set of clean patterns it’s happy to vibrate in: one hump, two humps, three humps, and so on. These patterns are called modes, and the points that never move are called nodes.


Code
x = np.linspace(0, L, 1000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(8, 6), sharex=True)
for n, ax in enumerate(axes, start=1):
    shape = np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L)
    ax.plot(x, shape, color="#534AB7", lw=2)
    ax.plot(x, -shape, color="#534AB7", lw=1, alpha=0.3)
    ax.plot(np.arange(n + 1) * L / n, np.zeros(n + 1), "o", color="#D85A30", ms=5)
    ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3)
    ax.text(1.02, 0, f"{n} hump{'s' if n > 1 else ''}\n{n * f1:.0f} Hz", va="center", fontsize=9)
axes[-1].set_xlabel("position along the string")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The first four modes of a string. The solid and faint curves show the two extremes of each swing; the dots are nodes, points that never move.




Notice the frequencies on the right: 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz. They’re exactly the numbers the spectrum analyser showed. That’s not a coincidence, and it’s worth seeing why the pattern is so tidy, because the whole-number spacing is the thing the rest of this article runs on.
The ends of the string can’t move, so every mode has to fit a whole number of humps between them. Half a hump would mean one end moving. Each hump is half a wave, so a mode with \(n\) humps has a wavelength of \(2L/n\). Waves travel along a given string at one fixed speed \(v\), set by how tight and how heavy the string is, and frequency is simply speed divided by wavelength:
\[f_n = \frac{v}{2L/n} = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n f_1 .\]
So mode 2 vibrates at exactly twice the frequency of mode 1, mode 3 at exactly three times, and so on. No in-betweens, no exceptions. That one line explains the spectrum.
There’s one more thing about modes that matters later. They’re the only shapes that keep their shape while vibrating. The string pulls itself back toward straight, and it pulls hardest wherever it’s bent most. In a smooth hump, the most bent part is also the part furthest out, so every point gets pulled back in proportion to how far out it is. They all reach the middle together, swing out the other side together, and the shape survives. Any other shape gets pulled unevenly and changes as it moves.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
A pluck is a triangle
When you pluck a string, you don’t pick a mode. You hook the string with your finger, pull it into a triangle, and let go.
A triangle isn’t any of those clean patterns. Its straight sides aren’t bent at all, so they feel no pull, while the corner feels a lot. So how does a triangle vibrate?
The answer comes from Joseph Fourier, and it’s one of the most useful ideas in physics: any shape can be built by stacking modes on top of each other.
\[\text{triangle}(x) = b_1 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) + b_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + b_3 \sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right) + \cdots\]
Each \(b_n\) says how much of mode \(n\) is in the triangle. Working them out is easier than it looks, because the modes don’t overlap with each other. Mathematically they’re orthogonal, the same way the \(x\) and \(y\) axes are: you can measure how far a point is along \(x\) without caring about \(y\). In the same way, you can measure how much of mode 3 is in the triangle without caring about any of the others. You multiply the triangle by the mode and add up the result along the string, which is what the integral in the code does.


Code
def triangle(x, p, h=1.0):
    """A string pulled up to height h at position p, straight lines to both ends."""
    return np.where(x < p, h * x / p, h * (L - x) / (L - p))

def coefficients(p, N):
    """How much of each mode 1..N is in the triangle: multiply by the mode, add up along the string."""
    n = np.arange(1, N + 1)[:, None]
    return 2 / L * integrate(triangle(x, p) * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L), x, axis=1)

p = 0.2                        # pluck a fifth of the way along the string
b = coefficients(p, 200)
tidy = lambda v: 0.0 if abs(v) < 5e-5 else v      # hide floating-point noise like -0.0000
for n in range(1, 8):
    print(f"mode {n}: b = {tidy(b[n-1]):+.4f}")


mode 1: b = +0.7444
mode 2: b = +0.3011
mode 3: b = +0.1338
mode 4: b = +0.0465
mode 5: b = +0.0000
mode 6: b = -0.0207
mode 7: b = -0.0246


Mode 1 dominates, mode 2 is about a third as big, and they shrink from there. Mode 5 comes out as zero, which looks odd but has a simple reason that we’ll get to.
Now stack them back up and watch the triangle reappear:


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, N in zip(axes.flat, [1, 3, 10, 50]):
    partial = sum(b[n-1] * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L) for n in range(1, N + 1))
    ax.plot(x, triangle(x, p), "--", color="0.6", label="the pluck")
    ax.plot(x, partial, color="#534AB7", lw=2, label=f"first {N} mode{'s' if N > 1 else ''}")
    for n in range(1, min(N, 4) + 1):
        ax.plot(x, b[n-1] * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L), color="#1D9E75", lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{N} mode{'s' if N > 1 else ''}", fontsize=10)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
fig.supxlabel("position along the string")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Adding modes one by one rebuilds the plucked triangle. One mode already gets the overall shape; the rest are mostly spent sharpening the corner.




The straight sides come together quickly. The sharp corner is what takes all the extra modes, since you can’t make a sharp point out of a few smooth curves.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Letting go
So the triangle is a stack of modes. When you let go, each mode does exactly what modes do: it swings back and forth in place at its own frequency, ignoring all the others. The string’s motion is just the sum of all those swings:
\[u(x,t) = \sum_n b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos(2\pi n f_1 t).\]
Each mode swings back and forth (that’s the cosine) at its own rate \(n f_1\).
I found this confusing at first, so it’s worth spelling out. The string isn’t vibrating in several places at once. It has one shape at every moment. That one shape just happens to be a sum of modes, and each piece of the sum keeps its own rhythm. Here’s what the sum looks like over one cycle:


Code
n = np.arange(1, 201)[:, None]
modes = b[:, None] * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(11, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, frac in zip(axes.flat, np.linspace(0, 1, 8)):
    shape = (modes * np.cos(2 * np.pi * n * frac)).sum(axis=0)
    ax.plot(x, shape, color="#534AB7", lw=2)
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.85", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_title(f"{frac:.2f} of a cycle", fontsize=9); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





One cycle of a plucked string. Each frame is a single shape; it’s built from 200 modes, each ticking at its own rate. The corner splits into two kinks that run back and forth, and after one full cycle the triangle comes back.




Real strings really do move like this. Film one in slow motion and you see the kink racing back and forth, not neat humps. The humps are the recipe; the kink is what the recipe cooks.
And the last frame is the reason you hear a single note. Every mode vibrates at a whole-number multiple of \(f_1\), so after exactly \(1/f_1\) of a second every one of them has finished a whole number of swings at the same instant. The triangle is back where it started, and the pattern repeats. It repeats 110 times a second, so that’s the pitch.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
What reaches your ear
A string on its own makes almost no sound. It’s far too thin to push much air. What you hear is the guitar’s bridge and body, which the string shakes. The bridge gets tugged by the slope of the string where the string meets it, and taking the slope of mode \(n\) multiplies it by \(n\). So the strength of each harmonic in the sound is proportional to \(n\,b_n\) rather than \(b_n\).
Here’s that signal turned into sound, with the higher harmonics fading a little faster than the low ones, as they do on a real string. Headphones help, because small speakers struggle with 110 Hz.


Code
t = np.arange(int(fs * 2.0)) / fs

def pluck_sound(p, n_max=40, decay=True, skip_fundamental=False):
    bp = coefficients(p, n_max)
    sig = np.zeros_like(t)
    for k in range(2 if skip_fundamental else 1, n_max + 1):
        fade = np.exp(-t * (1.2 + 0.25 * k)) if decay else 1.0     # higher harmonics die faster
        sig += k * bp[k-1] * fade * np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * f1 * t)  # bridge feels n * b_n
    return sig / np.max(np.abs(sig))

display(Audio(pluck_sound(p=0.2), rate=fs))



                
                    
                    Your browser does not support the audio element.
                
              


Now break that sound back into its frequencies, which is what the spectrum analyser in the introduction did:


Code
steady = pluck_sound(p=0.2, decay=False)
spectrum = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(steady * np.hanning(len(steady))))
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(steady), 1 / fs)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.2))
plt.plot(freqs, spectrum / spectrum.max(), color="#534AB7")
for k in range(1, 13):
    plt.axvline(k * f1, color="0.88", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
plt.xlim(0, 13 * f1)
plt.xticks([k * f1 for k in range(1, 13)], [f"{k * f1:.0f}" for k in range(1, 13)], fontsize=8)
plt.xlabel("frequency (Hz)"); plt.ylabel("relative strength")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The frequencies in our plucked string. Every peak sits at a whole-number multiple of 110 Hz, exactly as the mode argument predicted. Harmonics 5 and 10 are missing.




The peaks land exactly on 110, 220, 330 and so on. Nothing in the maths added them. They were in the triangle all along, and letting go of the string released each one at its own rate. Harmonics 5 and 10 are missing, which ties back to that zero coefficient for mode 5. Hold that thought.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
But isn’t Fourier just maths?
This is the part that bothered me. A Fourier decomposition is a calculation. Your ear can’t do integrals, so how can it possibly hear the separate harmonics?
The answer is resonance. Anything with a natural rhythm, like a child on a swing, a tuning fork or a wine glass, responds to pushes in a very particular way. Push a swing in time with its rhythm and every push adds to the motion, so it goes higher and higher. Push at some other rhythm and half your pushes arrive at the wrong moment and cancel the other half, and nothing much happens.
Now feed something with a natural frequency \(f_0\) a messy sound with lots of frequencies in it. The part of the sound at \(f_0\) keeps pushing at the right moment and builds up. Every other part drifts in and out of step and cancels itself. That build-up-or-cancel process is exactly the calculation behind a Fourier coefficient: multiply the signal by a wave at \(f_0\) and add up the result over time,
\[\int F(t)\cos(2\pi f_0 t)\,dt .\]
So a resonator is a physical machine that measures how much of one frequency is in a sound. Line up a few hundred of them, each tuned a little higher than the last, and you have a machine that measures the whole spectrum.
The code below does exactly that. It builds 580 simulated weights-on-springs, tuned from 50 to 1,500 Hz, and drives them all with the guitar sound. There’s no Fourier transform anywhere in it. It just pushes and pulls springs, one tiny time step after another.


Code
f0 = np.arange(50, 1500, 2.5)          # each spring's natural frequency
w0 = 2 * np.pi * f0
Q = 30                                 # how sharply each spring is tuned
drive = pluck_sound(p=0.2, decay=False)[: int(0.9 * fs)]
dt = 1 / fs

pos = np.zeros_like(f0); vel = np.zeros_like(f0); energy = np.zeros_like(f0)
settle = int(0.5 * fs)                 # wait for the springs to settle before measuring
for i, F in enumerate(drive):
    acc = F - (w0 / Q) * vel - w0**2 * pos     # push from the sound, minus friction, minus spring
    vel += acc * dt
    pos += vel * dt
    if i >= settle:
        energy += (w0**2 * pos) ** 2

response = np.sqrt(energy / (len(drive) - settle))
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.2))
plt.plot(f0, response / response.max(), color="#D85A30")
for k in range(1, 14):
    plt.axvline(k * f1, color="0.88", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
plt.xlabel("natural frequency of the spring (Hz)"); plt.ylabel("how hard it swings")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





580 simulated springs, each tuned to a different frequency, all driven by the same plucked-string sound. The ones tuned to a harmonic swing hard; the rest barely move. No Fourier transform was used.




The springs reproduce the spectrum almost exactly, missing harmonics included. Build something out of differently tuned resonators and it does a Fourier analysis just by existing.
Your inner ear is built on this principle. Inside the cochlea is a strip called the basilar membrane, about three and a half centimetres long, which is stiff and narrow at one end and wide and floppy at the other. Different spots along it respond to different frequencies, high at the narrow end and low at the wide end, and hair cells along its length report how much each spot is moving. By the time a sound reaches your brain, it has already been sorted by frequency. Helmholtz guessed at a version of this in 1863, and Georg von Békésy worked out how the membrane actually moves, which earned him the Nobel Prize in 1961. The real ear is messier than a bank of springs (it actively amplifies quiet sounds and also uses the timing of nerve signals), but the basic trick is the same.
So why does a plucked string sound like one note and not a chord? Because your brain takes any set of frequencies that are whole-number multiples of a common base, groups them into a single sound, and gives it the pitch of that base. The mix of harmonics becomes the timbre, the difference between a guitar and a clarinet playing the same A.
The grouping is so strong that the base frequency doesn’t even need to be there. Here’s the same pluck with the 110 Hz fundamental removed completely:


Code
display(Audio(pluck_sound(p=0.2, skip_fundamental=True), rate=fs))

It still sounds like the same note, just a bit thinner. Your brain fills in the missing 110 Hz from the spacing of the others. This is why a man’s voice on an old phone line still sounds low, even though the line cuts off everything below about 300 Hz. If you’re listening on laptop speakers, you’ve been hearing this effect all along, since they can barely play 110 Hz anyway.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Why some overtones are louder
Back to that missing fifth harmonic. Doing the integral by hand for a triangle pulled to height \(h\) at position \(p\) gives a formula for each coefficient:
\[b_n = \frac{2hL^2}{\pi^2 n^2\,p(L-p)}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi p}{L}\right).\]
It agrees with the numbers the code worked out earlier:


Code
formula = lambda n, p, h=1.0: 2 * h * L**2 * np.sin(n * np.pi * p / L) / (np.pi**2 * n**2 * p * (L - p))
for n in range(1, 8):
    print(f"mode {n}: code {tidy(b[n-1]):+.4f}   formula {tidy(formula(n, p)):+.4f}")


mode 1: code +0.7444   formula +0.7444
mode 2: code +0.3011   formula +0.3011
mode 3: code +0.1338   formula +0.1338
mode 4: code +0.0465   formula +0.0465
mode 5: code +0.0000   formula +0.0000
mode 6: code -0.0207   formula -0.0207
mode 7: code -0.0246   formula -0.0246


The formula is useful because it shows why the numbers come out the way they do. What reaches your ear goes like \(n\,b_n\), so the strength of harmonic \(n\) is proportional to
\[\frac{1}{n}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi p}{L}\right),\]
and each of the two pieces has a job.
The \(1/n\) is about how sharp the pluck is. Smooth shapes are made almost entirely of low modes; sharp corners need high ones. That’s why a pick or a fingernail sounds bright, while the soft flesh of your thumb rounds off the corner, removes high modes and sounds warm. A piano hammer works the same way, and since its felt gets harder the harder you hit, loud piano notes sound brighter as well as louder.
The sine is about where you pluck, and it explains the mystery. If you pluck exactly on a node of some mode, that mode can’t be started, because you’re pulling on the one point of it that never moves. We plucked at one fifth of the string, which is a node of mode 5 and of mode 10. So both were silent.


Code
ks = np.arange(1, 13)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3), sharey=True)
for ax, (pp, label) in zip(axes, [(0.5, "plucked in the middle"), (0.2, "a fifth of the way along"), (0.06, "near the bridge")]):
    s = np.abs(ks * coefficients(pp, 12)); s /= s.max()
    ax.bar(ks, s, color="#7F77DD")
    ax.set_title(label, fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks(ks)
axes[0].set_ylabel("relative strength"); fig.supxlabel("harmonic number")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





How loud each harmonic is for three pluck positions. Pluck in the middle and every even harmonic disappears; pluck near the end and the high harmonics stay strong.




Pluck in the middle and you’re sitting on a node of every even mode, so harmonics 2, 4, 6 and so on all vanish, which gives a hollow, round sound. Pluck near the bridge and the sine stays large for lots of harmonics, so the tone turns bright and twangy. You can hear the difference:


Code
display(Audio(pluck_sound(p=0.5), rate=fs))    # middle of the string: hollow
display(Audio(pluck_sound(p=0.06), rate=fs))   # near the bridge: bright

Guitarists use this constantly without thinking about it, moving their picking hand toward the soundhole for a warmer tone and toward the bridge for a sharper one.
The string isn’t the whole story, of course. Higher harmonics lose their energy faster, so a note gets darker as it rings out (that’s the fading in the sounds above). The guitar’s body and the piano’s soundboard have resonances of their own, boosting some harmonics and muting others. And real strings are a little stiff, which nudges the high harmonics slightly above exact whole-number multiples. But the pattern set by the pluck itself is what you’ve seen here.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Where this leaves us
Every note you play on a string instrument is really a stack of frequencies at 1, 2, 3, 4 times the note itself. Your ear separates them, and your brain fuses them back into one sound. That whole-number pattern is the part to remember, because it’s what lets two different notes share harmonics, and sharing harmonics is what makes them sound good together. That’s where the next section picks up.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
A rope example
Before tackling harmonics head on, it may be helpful to think of a guitar string as a rope tied to a post, with you holding the other end and shaking it.
If you shake it at just the right rhythm, the whole rope swings as one big loop. Shake twice as often and it snaps into two loops, with a point in the middle that stays still. Three times as often gives three loops. At any rates in between, no clean pattern builds up and the rope just jiggles. How often you shake is a frequency, and these special frequencies are exactly the fundamental and its harmonics.
In physics, these patterns are called modes, and the points that never move, including the two ends, are called nodes. An up-loop followed by a down-loop makes one full wave, and its length is called the wavelength \(\lambda\). So one loop is half a wavelength.
The figure below shows each mode as a snapshot. In reality, each loop keeps flipping between up and down, while the dots stay perfectly still.





The first four modes of a string with a fundamental \(f_1\) of 110 Hz. The dots are nodes, and \(n\) is the number of loops. Each color marks one full wavelength, so at \(n = 1\) the string holds only half a wavelength.










NoteWatch this for a visual demonstration.









Notice that the frequencies in the graph, 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz, are all multiples of 110. So then, why specifically multiples?
Suppose the string has length \(L\). Both ends are held fixed on the resting line, the straight line the string lies along when it’s still, so the wave pattern has to start and end on the ends.
Starting from the resting line at the left end, the pattern only returns to it at the end of each loop. If the string’s length ended partway through a loop, the right end would be sitting above or below the line, which is physically impossible, as the ends are fixed.





Top: a pattern with 2 loops starts and ends on the resting line, so it fits the string. Bottom: a pattern with 2.5 loops ends at a peak, leaving the right end displaced (arrow).




So a mode must contain a whole number of loops. To write this as a formula, recall that one loop is half a wavelength. A mode with \(n\) loops therefore fills the string when:
\[
L = n \cdot \frac{\lambda}{2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\lambda = \frac{2L}{n}
\]
Even though the loops seem to stay in place, each pattern is really made of ripples running back and forth along the string, bouncing off the fixed ends. These ripples travel at one fixed speed \(v\), determined by the string’s tightness and weight.
For any wave, frequency is speed divided by wavelength: the faster the wave moves, or the shorter it is, the more times it vibrates each second. For mode \(n\), whose wavelength is \(\lambda_n = 2L/n\):
\[
f_n = \frac{v}{\lambda_n} = \frac{v}{2L/n} = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n f_1,
\qquad\text{where } f_1 = \frac{v}{2L}.
\]
The speed \(v\) and the length \(L\) are fixed by the string, so only \(n\) changes from mode to mode. For an ideal string, mode 2 therefore vibrates at exactly twice the frequency of mode 1, mode 3 at three times, and so on. (Real strings are slightly stiff, which nudges the higher harmonics a bit higher in frequency.) For our 110 Hz string, that gives 110, 220, 330 Hz.
This is also why turning a tuning peg changes the pitch: tightening the string makes waves travel faster, which raises \(v\), and with it every \(f_n\).
That settles the first question: a string can only vibrate cleanly at \(f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \ldots\). But in the rope example we only saw these patterns one at a time, each at a rhythm we chose. When we pluck a string, all these modes appear at the same time, each at a different strength. So what’s happening?

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Why Does
When you pluck a string, you don’t pick a mode. You hook the string with your finger, pull it into a triangle, and let go.
A triangle isn’t any of those clean patterns. Its straight sides aren’t bent at all, so they feel no pull, while the corner feels a lot. So how does a triangle vibrate?
The answer comes from Joseph Fourier, and it’s one of the most useful ideas in physics: any shape can be built by stacking modes on top of each other.
\[\text{triangle}(x) = b_1 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) + b_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + b_3 \sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right) + \cdots\]
Each \(b_n\) says how much of mode \(n\) is in the triangle. Working them out is easier than it looks, because the modes don’t overlap with each other. Mathematically they’re orthogonal, the same way the \(x\) and \(y\) axes are: you can measure how far a point is along \(x\) without caring about \(y\). In the same way, you can measure how much of mode 3 is in the triangle without caring about any of the others. You multiply the triangle by the mode and add up the result along the string, which is what the integral in the code does.


Code
def triangle(x, p, h=1.0):
    """A string pulled up to height h at position p, straight lines to both ends."""
    return np.where(x < p, h * x / p, h * (L - x) / (L - p))

def coefficients(p, N):
    """How much of each mode 1..N is in the triangle: multiply by the mode, add up along the string."""
    n = np.arange(1, N + 1)[:, None]
    return 2 / L * integrate(triangle(x, p) * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L), x, axis=1)

tidy = lambda v: 0.0 if abs(v) < 5e-5 else v      # hide floating-point noise like -0.0000
for n in range(1, 8):
    print(f"mode {n}: b = {tidy(b[n-1]):+.4f}")

The straight sides come together quickly. The sharp corner is what takes all the extra modes, since you can’t make a sharp point out of a few smooth curves.

title: On Harmonics.
section: Why are there multiple harmonics concurrently?
text:
Why are there multiple harmonics concurrently?
If you’ve seen those viral clips of a guitar string rippling in slow, lazy waves, you might now think the rope picture above is exactly what a guitar string does. And now, you are demanding a refund of your time from me, because if guitar vibrates like the rope, then where are the harmonics???
Not quite. Many of those clips are filmed on a phone held inside the guitar, and the ripples are an illusion: the camera captures the image line by line, top to bottom, while the string keeps moving.
So what does a plucked string really look like? Think about what your finger does. You are not shaking the string. Instead you hook it, pull it aside, and let go. Just before letting go, what do you think the shape is?
…
If you guess a triangle, you are exactly right.

title: What a plucked string actually does
text:
You hook a finger under a guitar string, pull it sideways and let go. Just before release the string is two straight lines meeting at your finger: a triangle. A tenth of a second later it’s ringing at 110 Hz, and your ear picks up 220, 330, 440 and higher as well.
This page answers three questions. What does the triangle do once you let go? Why do we end up describing it as a pile of sine waves? And how does that pile of sine waves turn into the overtones you hear? Each equation below answers one of those questions, and each one gets used in the code that follows it.

title: What a plucked string actually does
text:
The starting shape
Pluck at a point \(p\) along the string and pull it up by a height \(h\). The string is pinned at both ends, so it makes two straight lines:
\[
y_0(x) = \begin{cases} h\,\dfrac{x}{p} & 0 \le x \le p \\[2mm] h\,\dfrac{L-x}{L-p} & p \le x \le L \end{cases}
\]
The string isn’t moving yet, so its starting velocity is zero everywhere. Both facts matter later on.

def triangle(x, p, h=h):
    return np.where(x <= p, h * x / p, h * (L - x) / (L - p))

p = 0.2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.4))
ax.plot(x, triangle(x, p), color="k", lw=2)
ax.plot([0, L], [0, 0], "ko", ms=6)
ax.annotate("your finger", (p, h), (p + 0.12, h * 0.95), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
ax.set_xlabel("position along string"); ax.set_ylabel("displacement")
ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.2)
plt.show()




The string just before release, plucked a fifth of the way along.

title: What a plucked string actually does
section: What happens when you let go
text:
What happens when you let go
Think of the string as a chain of tiny beads, each tugged by its two neighbours through the tension. If the string is straight at a bead, the two tugs point in opposite directions and cancel, so the bead doesn’t move. If the string is bent there, the tugs no longer cancel, and the bead gets pulled toward straightening the bend. A sharper bend means a stronger pull.
That’s all the physics there is. In symbols, the acceleration of each point equals the bend (the curvature) at that point, times a constant:
\[
\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = c^2\,\frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}
\]
Here \(c\) is the speed at which a disturbance travels along the string. It’s set by the tension and how heavy the string is.
Now look at the triangle with this rule in mind. The two straight sections have no bend at all, so at the instant of release they feel no force and don’t move. All of the bend is concentrated at the corner, so that’s where all the motion starts. The corner can’t stay where it is. It splits in two, and the two halves run off in opposite directions.
We can check this without any Fourier maths. The code below applies the tug-of-neighbours rule directly to 500 beads and steps it forward in time.

def simulate(y0, steps):
    """Step the wave equation forward on a grid of beads. Start at rest.
    Uses c*dt = dx, for which this simple scheme is exact on the grid."""
    prev = y0.copy()
    curr = y0.copy()
    curr[1:-1] = 0.5 * (y0[2:] + y0[:-2])        # first step from rest
    frames = [prev.copy(), curr.copy()]
    for _ in range(steps - 1):
        nxt = np.zeros_like(curr)
        nxt[1:-1] = curr[2:] + curr[:-2] - prev[1:-1]
        prev, curr = curr, nxt
        frames.append(curr.copy())
    return np.array(frames)

# with c*dt = dx, the wave crosses the string in M steps, and one full period is 2M steps
step_ms = (T / (2 * M)) * 1000

Watch the two strings and they behave completely differently.
The sine never changes shape. It shrinks, goes flat, comes back upside down and grows again, and its still points (the nodes, at a third and two thirds of the way along) never move. It does this three times in the period shown, because a three-loop sine vibrates at three times the fundamental. At every moment it’s the starting shape scaled by some number between −1 and 1. That’s what having a single frequency looks like.
The triangle keeps changing shape. At the instant of release the corner splits in two. One half runs left, hits the end, and comes back upside down. The other half runs right. The straight pieces between them tilt and slide. Halfway through the period the string is the starting triangle mirrored and flipped, with the corner at 0.8 and pointing down. After one full period it’s back where it started. At no point in between is it a scaled copy of the triangle, so there’s no single frequency describing its motion.

title: What a plucked string actually does
text:
Why sine waves?
So which shapes behave like the sine on the left, keeping their shape and only changing size? Call such a shape \(X(x)\). For it to only change size, every point has to accelerate back toward zero in proportion to how far out it is, so all the points stay in step. By the bead rule, acceleration is set by the bend. So the bend at each point has to be proportional to the displacement there, and pointing back toward zero:
\[
X''(x) = -k^2\,X(x)
\]
Only one family of functions has its curvature equal to minus a multiple of itself: sines and cosines. The ends are pinned, so \(X(0) = X(L) = 0\). That rules out cosines and only allows sines that fit a whole number of half-waves between the ends:
\[
X_n(x) = \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
\]
These are the string’s modes. Each one swings up and down at a single frequency, and fitting \(n\) half-waves into the string makes it \(n\) times faster than the first:
\[
f_n = n\,f_1
\]
That’s where the harmonic series 110, 220, 330, … comes from. Those are the only frequencies at which the string can vibrate while keeping its shape.
The triangle is not one of these shapes. Its curvature is zero along the straight parts and infinite at the corner, which is nothing like “minus a multiple of itself”. That’s why it can’t move with one frequency.
The way out is this. The pulls on a bead simply add, so if the string’s shape is a sum of pieces, its motion is the sum of each piece’s motion. So if we can write the triangle as a sum of modes, each mode does its own easy thing (bob up and down at \(n f_1\)), and adding them back up gives the motion of the whole string. Breaking the triangle into sines isn’t a mathematical convenience we chose. It’s how you turn one hard problem into many easy ones, because sines are the only shapes whose motion is easy.

title: What a plucked string actually does
text:
How much of each mode?
We want numbers \(b_1, b_2, b_3, \dots\) such that
\[
y_0(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
\]
To find one of them, say \(b_3\), we need to isolate the third mode from all the others. The modes have a useful property here. If you multiply two different modes together and add up the product along the string, you get exactly zero. Their ups and downs cancel. A mode multiplied by itself gives \(L/2\). So multiplying the whole sum by \(\sin(3\pi x/L)\) and adding along the string wipes out every term except the third:
\[
b_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L y_0(x)\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx
\]
Here’s that cancellation checked numerically, followed by the recipe applied to the triangle.

modes = np.array([np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L) for n in range(1, 6)])
overlap = np.array([[integrate(a * b, x) for b in modes] for a in modes])
print("Multiply mode i by mode j and add up along the string (first 5 modes):")
print(np.round(overlap, 4) + 0.0)   # "+ 0.0" turns -0.0 into 0.0

Multiply mode i by mode j and add up along the string (first 5 modes):
[[0.5 0.  0.  0.  0. ]
 [0.  0.5 0.  0.  0. ]
 [0.  0.  0.5 0.  0. ]
 [0.  0.  0.  0.5 0. ]
 [0.  0.  0.  0.  0.5]]


Every off-diagonal entry is zero, and every diagonal entry is \(L/2 = 0.5\).

def coefficients(p, N, h=h):
    """b_n for n = 1..N, by the projection recipe above (numerical integration)."""
    y0 = triangle(x, p, h)
    return np.array([2 / L * integrate(y0 * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L), x)
                     for n in range(1, N + 1)])

def b_formula(n, p, h=h):
    """The same thing, done by hand for a triangle."""
    return 2 * h * L**2 / (np.pi**2 * n**2 * p * (L - p)) * np.sin(n * np.pi * p / L)

n = np.arange(1, 11)
b_num = coefficients(p, 10)
for k, bn, bf in zip(n, b_num, b_formula(n, p)):
    bn, bf = round(bn, 4) + 0.0, round(bf, 4) + 0.0   # avoid printing -0.0000
    print(f"mode {k:2d}:  by integration {bn:+.4f}   by formula {bf:+.4f}")

The formula in that function is the integral done by hand for a triangle:
\[
b_n = \frac{2hL^2}{\pi^2 n^2\, p(L-p)}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi p}{L}\right)
\]
It has two parts, and each one explains something you can hear.

The \(1/n^2\). Higher modes are needed, but less and less. The triangle is smooth everywhere except at one corner, and the high modes are there only to build that corner.
The \(\sin(n\pi p/L)\). This is the value of mode \(n\) at the pluck point. If the pluck point sits on one of mode \(n\)’s nodes, that mode gets nothing. At \(p = 0.2\), mode 5 has a node exactly at 0.2, so \(b_5 = 0\) (and \(b_{10}\) too). Pluck in the middle and every even mode vanishes.

title: What a plucked string actually does
text:
Building the triangle back up
Now let’s add the modes one at a time and watch the triangle appear. In each panel the colours run from dark (just the first mode) to bright (many modes).

def partial_sum(p, N):
    b = b_formula(np.arange(1, N + 1), p)
    return sum(b[k] * np.sin((k + 1) * np.pi * x / L) for k in range(N))

Ns = [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50]
colors = plt.cm.plasma(np.linspace(0, 0.9, len(Ns)))

for ax, pp in zip(axes, [0.5, 0.75, 0.95]):

        ax.plot(x, partial_sum(pp, N), color=c, lw=1.4, label=f"{N} mode{'s' if N > 1 else ''}")
    ax.plot(x, triangle(x, pp), "k", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.25); ax.set_title(f"plucked at {pp}", fontsize=10, loc="left")
axes[0].legend(ncol=4, fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
axes[1].set_ylabel("displacement of string")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("position along string")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()




Partial sums of the sine series for three pluck points. Dark = few modes, bright = many. Black = the actual triangle.




Three things stand out.

One mode already gets you most of the way there. For a centre pluck, the first mode alone is about 81% of the pluck height (\(8/\pi^2\)), and the triangle is already recognisable after three modes.
The closer to the end you pluck, the more modes you need. A pluck at 0.95 has a steep, narrow corner. The early modes are too broad to make it, and the corner only sharpens once dozens of short modes pile up. Plucking near the bridge gives a brighter, thinner sound for exactly this reason: more of the energy is in the high modes.
The corner is the last thing to form. Away from the corner, a handful of modes already sit on top of the triangle. All the work of the high modes goes into that one sharp point.

Here’s how fast the error shrinks for the \(p=0.2\) pluck. It roughly halves each time you double the number of modes, which is the \(1/n^2\) at work.

title: What a plucked string actually does
text:
Letting it go
Now we know two things: each mode bobs at its own frequency, and how much of each mode the triangle contains. The string starts at rest, so each mode starts at full height and swings like a cosine. Adding them back up gives the motion of the whole string:
\[
y(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos(2\pi n f_1 t)
\]
This prediction came out of the Fourier series. The bead simulation from earlier never heard of sines. If the reasoning above is right, the two should agree.

def string_at(t, p, N=200, decay=None):
    n = np.arange(1, N + 1)
    b = b_formula(n, p)
    amp = b * np.cos(2 * np.pi * n * f1 * t)
    if decay is not None:
        amp = amp * np.exp(-decay(n) * t)
    return amp @ np.sin(np.outer(n, np.pi * x / L))

tri_run = simulate(triangle(xg, p), 2 * M)
steps = [0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500]
colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0, 0.9, len(steps)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))

title: What a plucked string actually does
section: A real string: the corner wears off
text:
A real string: the corner wears off
Everything so far is a frictionless string, and it would keep its two travelling corners forever. A real string loses energy: to the air, to internal friction and stiffness in the wire, and through the bridge into the body of the instrument (which is how you hear it at all). These losses hit the high modes much harder than the low ones.
To show what that does, give mode \(n\) a fade-out rate \(\gamma_n\) that grows with \(n\):
\[
y(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\, e^{-\gamma_n t} \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos(2\pi n f_1 t)
\]
The rates I use below (\(\gamma_n = 1.5 + 0.08\,n^2\) per second) are made up so the effect is easy to see. They are not measured from a real guitar, and real values depend on the string, the instrument and where you pluck. What I’d trust is the pattern: the high modes go first.

decay = lambda n: 1.5 + 0.08 * n**2

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
tt = np.linspace(0, 1.0, 400)
# (modes 5, 10, 15, 20 are absent for a pluck at 0.2, so pick ones that exist)
for k in [1, 2, 3, 9, 19]:
    left.semilogy(tt * 1000, np.abs(b_formula(k, p)) * np.exp(-decay(k) * tt), label=f"mode {k}")
left.set_xlabel("time after pluck (ms)"); left.set_ylabel("amplitude of mode")
left.set_ylim(1e-4, 1); left.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False)

for ms, c in zip([0, 50, 200, 1000], plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0, 0.85, 4))):
    t = round(ms / 1000 / T) * T                # a whole number of periods: top of the swing
    y = string_at(t, p, decay=decay)
    right.plot(x, y / y.max(), color=c, lw=2, label=f"{ms} ms")
right.plot(x, np.sin(np.pi * x / L), "k--", lw=1, label="pure sine")
right.set_xlabel("position along string"); right.set_ylabel("shape (scaled)")
right.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for k in [1, 2, 3, 9, 19, 39]:
    print(f"mode {k:2d} falls to 37% of its start in about {1000/decay(k):.0f} ms")




Left: how fast each mode fades (illustrative rates). Right: the string at the top of its swing at four moments, each scaled to the same height so you can compare shapes. Dashed: a pure sine.




mode  1 falls to 37% of its start in about 633 ms
mode  2 falls to 37% of its start in about 549 ms
mode  3 falls to 37% of its start in about 450 ms
mode  9 falls to 37% of its start in about 125 ms
mode 19 falls to 37% of its start in about 33 ms
mode 39 falls to 37% of its start in about 8 ms


Over the first couple of tenths of a second the corner wears away. Modes in the high teens and above are almost gone by then, and the sharp point turns into a rounded hump. That rounding is also why a pluck starts bright and mellows: the high harmonics you hear in the attack are the corner, and as the corner dissolves they fade.
What doesn’t happen quickly is the string becoming a pure sine. The shape is still lopsided after a full second, because modes 2 and 3 are large to begin with (about 40% and 18% of mode 1 here) and fade almost as slowly as mode 1. The string ends up as a smooth, lopsided hump that is mostly mode 1, not a perfect sine.

title: What a plucked string actually does
section: So why does it look like a sine in slow motion?
text:
So why does it look like a sine in slow motion?
Partly because, as the plots above show, mode 1 dominates from the start, and once the corner has rounded off a smooth hump is what’s left. But mostly it’s the camera.
An A string goes through 110 cycles a second. A phone in slow-motion mode records about 240 frames a second, which is barely two frames per cycle, and each frame is smeared over part of a swing. You aren’t seeing the string’s shape at an instant. You’re seeing a smear of where it has been during each exposure, sampled so coarsely that consecutive frames land almost half a cycle apart. That kind of recording throws away fine detail such as a small corner racing along the string, and keeps the big, slow part of the motion, which is mode 1. To see the corner you need footage shot at several thousand frames per second, and then only in the first moments after the pluck, before it rounds off.

title: What a plucked string actually does
section: The whole story in one paragraph
text:
The whole story in one paragraph
Releasing a triangle can’t produce a single clean vibration, because only sine-shaped strings vibrate at one frequency, and a triangle isn’t a sine. So the string’s motion is a mixture of its sine-shaped modes, and the triangle decides how much of each: mostly the first, then less and less of the higher ones (\(1/n^2\)), with any mode that has a node at your finger left out entirely. Each mode vibrates at its own whole-number multiple of the fundamental, so the sound contains 110, 220, 330 Hz and up. Those are the overtones. The high modes build the sharp corner, and they’re the first to die, which is why the pluck’s bright attack fades into a rounder tone.

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
Pluck the open A string on a guitar and a tuner will tell you it’s 110 Hz. The string swings back and forth 110 times a second, and that’s the note you hear.
Run the same sound through a spectrum analyser, though, and you get a surprise. There isn’t one frequency in there. There’s 110 Hz, but also 220, 330, 440, 550, and on up, each a little quieter than the last. Those extra frequencies are the overtones, or harmonics, and the rest of this article depends on them. So it’s worth understanding where they come from, why your ear picks them up, and why some are louder than others.
There’s some maths below, but every equation is there to answer a specific question. There’s also Python, so you can run everything and check it yourself.
Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Audio, display

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
integrate = getattr(np, "trapezoid", None) or np.trapz   # the name differs between NumPy versions

L = 1.0        # string length (units don't matter here)
f1 = 110.0     # open A string, in Hz
fs = 44100     # audio sample rate

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
Shaking a rope
Tie one end of a rope to a post and shake the other end. Shake slowly and the whole rope swings as one big loop. Shake twice as fast and it snaps into two loops, with a point in the middle that stays still. Three times as fast gives three loops. Shake at any rhythm in between and you don’t get a clean pattern at all; the rope just flails.
A guitar string behaves the same way, except both ends are fixed instead of one being in your hand. It has a set of clean patterns it’s happy to vibrate in: one hump, two humps, three humps, and so on. These patterns are called modes, and the points that never move are called nodes.


Code
x = np.linspace(0, L, 1000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(8, 6), sharex=True)
for n, ax in enumerate(axes, start=1):
    shape = np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L)
    ax.plot(x, shape, color="#534AB7", lw=2)
    ax.plot(x, -shape, color="#534AB7", lw=1, alpha=0.3)
    ax.plot(np.arange(n + 1) * L / n, np.zeros(n + 1), "o", color="#D85A30", ms=5)
    ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3)
    ax.text(1.02, 0, f"{n} hump{'s' if n > 1 else ''}\n{n * f1:.0f} Hz", va="center", fontsize=9)
axes[-1].set_xlabel("position along the string")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The first four modes of a string. The solid and faint curves show the two extremes of each swing; the dots are nodes, points that never move.




Notice the frequencies on the right: 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz. They’re exactly the numbers the spectrum analyser showed. That’s not a coincidence, and it’s worth seeing why the pattern is so tidy, because the whole-number spacing is the thing the rest of this article runs on.
The ends of the string can’t move, so every mode has to fit a whole number of humps between them. Half a hump would mean one end moving. Each hump is half a wave, so a mode with \(n\) humps has a wavelength of \(2L/n\). Waves travel along a given string at one fixed speed \(v\), set by how tight and how heavy the string is, and frequency is simply speed divided by wavelength:
\[f_n = \frac{v}{2L/n} = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n f_1 .\]
So mode 2 vibrates at exactly twice the frequency of mode 1, mode 3 at exactly three times, and so on. No in-betweens, no exceptions. That one line explains the spectrum.
There’s one more thing about modes that matters later. They’re the only shapes that keep their shape while vibrating. The string pulls itself back toward straight, and it pulls hardest wherever it’s bent most. In a smooth hump, the most bent part is also the part furthest out, so every point gets pulled back in proportion to how far out it is. They all reach the middle together, swing out the other side together, and the shape survives. Any other shape gets pulled unevenly and changes as it moves.

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
A pluck is a triangle
When you pluck a string, you don’t pick a mode. You hook the string with your finger, pull it into a triangle, and let go.
A triangle isn’t any of those clean patterns. Its straight sides aren’t bent at all, so they feel no pull, while the corner feels a lot. So how does a triangle vibrate?
The answer comes from Joseph Fourier, and it’s one of the most useful ideas in physics: any shape can be built by stacking modes on top of each other.
\[\text{triangle}(x) = b_1 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) + b_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + b_3 \sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right) + \cdots\]
Each \(b_n\) says how much of mode \(n\) is in the triangle. Working them out is easier than it looks, because the modes don’t overlap with each other. Mathematically they’re orthogonal, the same way the \(x\) and \(y\) axes are: you can measure how far a point is along \(x\) without caring about \(y\). In the same way, you can measure how much of mode 3 is in the triangle without caring about any of the others. You multiply the triangle by the mode and add up the result along the string, which is what the integral in the code does.


Code
def triangle(x, p, h=1.0):
    """A string pulled up to height h at position p, straight lines to both ends."""
    return np.where(x < p, h * x / p, h * (L - x) / (L - p))

def coefficients(p, N):
    """How much of each mode 1..N is in the triangle: multiply by the mode, add up along the string."""
    n = np.arange(1, N + 1)[:, None]
    return 2 / L * integrate(triangle(x, p) * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L), x, axis=1)

p = 0.2                        # pluck a fifth of the way along the string
b = coefficients(p, 200)
tidy = lambda v: 0.0 if abs(v) < 5e-5 else v      # hide floating-point noise like -0.0000
for n in range(1, 8):
    print(f"mode {n}: b = {tidy(b[n-1]):+.4f}")


mode 1: b = +0.7444
mode 2: b = +0.3011
mode 3: b = +0.1338
mode 4: b = +0.0465
mode 5: b = +0.0000
mode 6: b = -0.0207
mode 7: b = -0.0246


Mode 1 dominates, mode 2 is about a third as big, and they shrink from there. Mode 5 comes out as zero, which looks odd but has a simple reason that we’ll get to.
Now stack them back up and watch the triangle reappear:


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, N in zip(axes.flat, [1, 3, 10, 50]):
    partial = sum(b[n-1] * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L) for n in range(1, N + 1))
    ax.plot(x, triangle(x, p), "--", color="0.6", label="the pluck")
    ax.plot(x, partial, color="#534AB7", lw=2, label=f"first {N} mode{'s' if N > 1 else ''}")
    for n in range(1, min(N, 4) + 1):
        ax.plot(x, b[n-1] * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L), color="#1D9E75", lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{N} mode{'s' if N > 1 else ''}", fontsize=10)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
fig.supxlabel("position along the string")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Adding modes one by one rebuilds the plucked triangle. One mode already gets the overall shape; the rest are mostly spent sharpening the corner.




The straight sides come together quickly. The sharp corner is what takes all the extra modes, since you can’t make a sharp point out of a few smooth curves.

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
Letting go
So the triangle is a stack of modes. When you let go, each mode does exactly what modes do: it swings back and forth in place at its own frequency, ignoring all the others. The string’s motion is just the sum of all those swings:
\[u(x,t) = \sum_n b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos(2\pi n f_1 t).\]
Each mode swings back and forth (that’s the cosine) at its own rate \(n f_1\).
I found this confusing at first, so it’s worth spelling out. The string isn’t vibrating in several places at once. It has one shape at every moment. That one shape just happens to be a sum of modes, and each piece of the sum keeps its own rhythm. Here’s what the sum looks like over one cycle:


Code
n = np.arange(1, 201)[:, None]
modes = b[:, None] * np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(11, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, frac in zip(axes.flat, np.linspace(0, 1, 8)):
    shape = (modes * np.cos(2 * np.pi * n * frac)).sum(axis=0)
    ax.plot(x, shape, color="#534AB7", lw=2)
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.85", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_title(f"{frac:.2f} of a cycle", fontsize=9); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





One cycle of a plucked string. Each frame is a single shape; it’s built from 200 modes, each ticking at its own rate. The corner splits into two kinks that run back and forth, and after one full cycle the triangle comes back.




Real strings really do move like this. Film one in slow motion and you see the kink racing back and forth, not neat humps. The humps are the recipe; the kink is what the recipe cooks.
And the last frame is the reason you hear a single note. Every mode vibrates at a whole-number multiple of \(f_1\), so after exactly \(1/f_1\) of a second every one of them has finished a whole number of swings at the same instant. The triangle is back where it started, and the pattern repeats. It repeats 110 times a second, so that’s the pitch.

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
What reaches your ear
A string on its own makes almost no sound. It’s far too thin to push much air. What you hear is the guitar’s bridge and body, which the string shakes. The bridge gets tugged by the slope of the string where the string meets it, and taking the slope of mode \(n\) multiplies it by \(n\). So the strength of each harmonic in the sound is proportional to \(n\,b_n\) rather than \(b_n\).
Here’s that signal turned into sound, with the higher harmonics fading a little faster than the low ones, as they do on a real string. Headphones help, because small speakers struggle with 110 Hz.


Code
t = np.arange(int(fs * 2.0)) / fs

def pluck_sound(p, n_max=40, decay=True, skip_fundamental=False):
    bp = coefficients(p, n_max)
    sig = np.zeros_like(t)
    for k in range(2 if skip_fundamental else 1, n_max + 1):
        fade = np.exp(-t * (1.2 + 0.25 * k)) if decay else 1.0     # higher harmonics die faster
        sig += k * bp[k-1] * fade * np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * f1 * t)  # bridge feels n * b_n
    return sig / np.max(np.abs(sig))

display(Audio(pluck_sound(p=0.2), rate=fs))



                
                    
                    Your browser does not support the audio element.
                
              


Now break that sound back into its frequencies, which is what the spectrum analyser in the introduction did:


Code
steady = pluck_sound(p=0.2, decay=False)
spectrum = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(steady * np.hanning(len(steady))))
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(steady), 1 / fs)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.2))
plt.plot(freqs, spectrum / spectrum.max(), color="#534AB7")
for k in range(1, 13):
    plt.axvline(k * f1, color="0.88", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
plt.xlim(0, 13 * f1)
plt.xticks([k * f1 for k in range(1, 13)], [f"{k * f1:.0f}" for k in range(1, 13)], fontsize=8)
plt.xlabel("frequency (Hz)"); plt.ylabel("relative strength")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The frequencies in our plucked string. Every peak sits at a whole-number multiple of 110 Hz, exactly as the mode argument predicted. Harmonics 5 and 10 are missing.




The peaks land exactly on 110, 220, 330 and so on. Nothing in the maths added them. They were in the triangle all along, and letting go of the string released each one at its own rate. Harmonics 5 and 10 are missing, which ties back to that zero coefficient for mode 5. Hold that thought.

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
But isn’t Fourier just maths?
This is the part that bothered me. A Fourier decomposition is a calculation. Your ear can’t do integrals, so how can it possibly hear the separate harmonics?
The answer is resonance. Anything with a natural rhythm, like a child on a swing, a tuning fork or a wine glass, responds to pushes in a very particular way. Push a swing in time with its rhythm and every push adds to the motion, so it goes higher and higher. Push at some other rhythm and half your pushes arrive at the wrong moment and cancel the other half, and nothing much happens.
Now feed something with a natural frequency \(f_0\) a messy sound with lots of frequencies in it. The part of the sound at \(f_0\) keeps pushing at the right moment and builds up. Every other part drifts in and out of step and cancels itself. That build-up-or-cancel process is exactly the calculation behind a Fourier coefficient: multiply the signal by a wave at \(f_0\) and add up the result over time,
\[\int F(t)\cos(2\pi f_0 t)\,dt .\]
So a resonator is a physical machine that measures how much of one frequency is in a sound. Line up a few hundred of them, each tuned a little higher than the last, and you have a machine that measures the whole spectrum.
The code below does exactly that. It builds 580 simulated weights-on-springs, tuned from 50 to 1,500 Hz, and drives them all with the guitar sound. There’s no Fourier transform anywhere in it. It just pushes and pulls springs, one tiny time step after another.


Code
f0 = np.arange(50, 1500, 2.5)          # each spring's natural frequency
w0 = 2 * np.pi * f0
Q = 30                                 # how sharply each spring is tuned
drive = pluck_sound(p=0.2, decay=False)[: int(0.9 * fs)]
dt = 1 / fs

pos = np.zeros_like(f0); vel = np.zeros_like(f0); energy = np.zeros_like(f0)
settle = int(0.5 * fs)                 # wait for the springs to settle before measuring
for i, F in enumerate(drive):
    acc = F - (w0 / Q) * vel - w0**2 * pos     # push from the sound, minus friction, minus spring
    vel += acc * dt
    pos += vel * dt
    if i >= settle:
        energy += (w0**2 * pos) ** 2

response = np.sqrt(energy / (len(drive) - settle))
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.2))
plt.plot(f0, response / response.max(), color="#D85A30")
for k in range(1, 14):
    plt.axvline(k * f1, color="0.88", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
plt.xlabel("natural frequency of the spring (Hz)"); plt.ylabel("how hard it swings")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()





580 simulated springs, each tuned to a different frequency, all driven by the same plucked-string sound. The ones tuned to a harmonic swing hard; the rest barely move. No Fourier transform was used.




The springs reproduce the spectrum almost exactly, missing harmonics included. Build something out of differently tuned resonators and it does a Fourier analysis just by existing.
Your inner ear is built on this principle. Inside the cochlea is a strip called the basilar membrane, about three and a half centimetres long, which is stiff and narrow at one end and wide and floppy at the other. Different spots along it respond to different frequencies, high at the narrow end and low at the wide end, and hair cells along its length report how much each spot is moving. By the time a sound reaches your brain, it has already been sorted by frequency. Helmholtz guessed at a version of this in 1863, and Georg von Békésy worked out how the membrane actually moves, which earned him the Nobel Prize in 1961. The real ear is messier than a bank of springs (it actively amplifies quiet sounds and also uses the timing of nerve signals), but the basic trick is the same.
So why does a plucked string sound like one note and not a chord? Because your brain takes any set of frequencies that are whole-number multiples of a common base, groups them into a single sound, and gives it the pitch of that base. The mix of harmonics becomes the timbre, the difference between a guitar and a clarinet playing the same A.
The grouping is so strong that the base frequency doesn’t even need to be there. Here’s the same pluck with the 110 Hz fundamental removed completely:


Code
display(Audio(pluck_sound(p=0.2, skip_fundamental=True), rate=fs))



                
                    
                    Your browser does not support the audio element.
                
              


It still sounds like the same note, just a bit thinner. Your brain fills in the missing 110 Hz from the spacing of the others. This is why a man’s voice on an old phone line still sounds low, even though the line cuts off everything below about 300 Hz. If you’re listening on laptop speakers, you’ve been hearing this effect all along, since they can barely play 110 Hz anyway.

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
Why some overtones are louder
Back to that missing fifth harmonic. Doing the integral by hand for a triangle pulled to height \(h\) at position \(p\) gives a formula for each coefficient:
\[b_n = \frac{2hL^2}{\pi^2 n^2\,p(L-p)}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi p}{L}\right).\]
It agrees with the numbers the code worked out earlier:


Code
formula = lambda n, p, h=1.0: 2 * h * L**2 * np.sin(n * np.pi * p / L) / (np.pi**2 * n**2 * p * (L - p))
for n in range(1, 8):
    print(f"mode {n}: code {tidy(b[n-1]):+.4f}   formula {tidy(formula(n, p)):+.4f}")


mode 1: code +0.7444   formula +0.7444
mode 2: code +0.3011   formula +0.3011
mode 3: code +0.1338   formula +0.1338
mode 4: code +0.0465   formula +0.0465
mode 5: code +0.0000   formula +0.0000
mode 6: code -0.0207   formula -0.0207
mode 7: code -0.0246   formula -0.0246


The formula is useful because it shows why the numbers come out the way they do. What reaches your ear goes like \(n\,b_n\), so the strength of harmonic \(n\) is proportional to
\[\frac{1}{n}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi p}{L}\right),\]
and each of the two pieces has a job.
The \(1/n\) is about how sharp the pluck is. Smooth shapes are made almost entirely of low modes; sharp corners need high ones. A piano hammer works the same way, and since its felt gets harder the harder you hit, loud piano notes sound brighter as well as louder.
The sine is about where you pluck, and it explains the mystery. If you pluck exactly on a node of some mode, that mode can’t be started, because you’re pulling on the one point of it that never moves. We plucked at one fifth of the string, which is a node of mode 5 and of mode 10. So both were silent.

title: Overtones: why one note is really many
text:
Where this leaves us
Every note you play on a string instrument is really a stack of frequencies at 1, 2, 3, 4 times the note itself. Your ear separates them, and your brain fuses them back into one sound. That whole-number pattern is the part to remember, because it’s what lets two different notes share harmonics, and sharing harmonics is what makes them sound good together. That’s where the next section picks up.

title: On Harmonics.
section: Where are the harmonics coming from?
text:
Where are the harmonics coming from?
In the rope example, each pattern needed its own shaking rhythm: one loop at one rhythm, two loops at twice that. But a pluck has no rhythm at all. You pull once and let go. So where do all those modes come from?
If you’ve seen those viral clips of a guitar string vibrating in slow, lazy waves, you might now think the rope example is exactly what a guitar string does. And now you are demanding a refund of your time from me, because if guitar vibrates like the rope, then how can there be harmonics when a wave can only vibrate at one frequency?!?!
Hear me out before you get your pitchfork. It’s not quite like that. Many of those clips are filmed on a phone held inside the guitar, and those ripples are an illusion. Phone camera captures the picture line by line rather than all at once, so different parts of the string are photographed at slightly different moments.






NoteWatch this video at 01:46 to see the illusion.









So what does a plucked string really look like? Think about what your finger does. You are not shaking the string. You hook it with your finger, pull and let go. At that moment, the string forms a triangle: it is no longer a smooth curve, but two straight lines meeting at a corner, right where your finger is.





A guitar string is actually a triangle now?




That corner is the key to unlocking the mystery behind harmonics. To see why, we first need a closer look at how a mode moves.
A mode only ever gets taller, shorter, or flipped upside down. Freeze it at any moment and you’ll see the same curve, just scaled. But at the end, it must return back to how it started. Therefore, a mode at any moment is a scaled version of its initial and final displacement. A sine wave is the only curve that has this special property.






NoteWhy only a sine wave?





A tight string naturally wants to straighten itself because of tension. Wherever it’s bent, it gets pulled toward the inside of the bend, and the sharper the bend, the harder the pull. A straight stretch feels no pull at all.
For a string to keep its shape, the pull has to be strongest where the string is farthest out and fade to nothing where it crosses the middle, so that every point reaches the resting line at the same time.
A sine wave has the special property where the bend at every position is proportional to its height. It is most sharply bent at its peaks, and perfectly straight where it crosses the line. Therefore, the force exerted toward the resting line is proportional to the height.



However, the triangle is not a sine wave. Look at the triangle, its straight sides feel no pull at all; the only bend is at the corner. As only at a bend is a force induced, the corner should start moving while the sides wait, and the triangle should not keep its shape.
Let’s test this prediction by releasing two strings side by side: one shaped like the third mode, and one shaped like the triangle.

The sine string behaves exactly as predicted: it only ever gets taller, shorter, or flipped. However, when the triangle is let go, its corner splits into two that run off in opposite directions, and the straight parts only start moving once a corner reaches them. Freeze it at any moment and you’ll see a different shape, not a scaled triangle.
But also, watch the clock. After exactly one period, about 9.1 ms, the two corners have bounced off the ends and met again where they started, and the triangle is back to its original shape again.
So the triangle isn’t a mode, yet its motion repeats at exactly the fundamental’s rhythm like how a fundamental would. That is a hint of what the triangle is.

text:
Fourier Series
For some bookkeeping, we need to introduce a few formula.
Suppose we pluck the string at position \(p\), pulling it up to height \(h\). The starting shape is a triangle (as shown in the demonstration before):
\[
\text{triangle}(x) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{h\,x}{p}, & 0 \le x \le p \\[1.5ex]
\dfrac{h\,(L - x)}{L - p}, & p < x \le L
\end{cases}
\]
Recall that each mode is a sine wave with \(n\) loops. The starting shape can be described as below:
\[
X_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
\]






NoteDerivation of the shape formula:





Transcribing to Latex will take forever.



In the 1750s, Daniel Bernoulli proposed that the motion of a string fixed at both ends is a sum of its modes. Not everyone was convinced, and Leonhard Euler and Jean d’Alembert certainly weren’t.
D’Alembert doubted that a corner was even allowed, since the equation for a vibrating string needs the string to be smoothly curved everywhere. Euler was happy to allow corners, after all, strings are plucked and harmonics are heard, but he couldn’t see how smooth sine waves could ever add up to one discontinued corners. If a finite sum of sines is smooth, then how can an infinite sum suddenly turn non-smooth? [1]
In the early 1800s, while studying how temperature changes over time inside a solid body, Joseph Fourier made an even bolder claim. He proposed that any shape can be written as a sum of sines, including our triangle. Mathematicians now call this a Fourier series. \[
\text{triangle}(x) = b_1 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) + b_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + b_3 \sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right) + \cdots = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
\]
Each \(b_n\) describes how much of mode \(n\) is in the triangle. In our case, we would like to find the different modes that together construct our triangle.
To find one of them, say \(b_3\), we need to isolate the third mode from all the others. We do this by exploiting a property of modes called orthogonality.






TipWhat is orthogonality?





Take two functions \(f\) and \(g\) on the string, \(0 \le x \le L\). Multiply their values at each point along the string, then add up all the results. This gives a single number, called the inner product \(\langle f, g \rangle\), defined as the integral \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^L f(x)\,g(x)\,dx\). If \(\langle f, g \rangle = 0\), we say \(f\) and \(g\) are orthogonal.
The modes are orthogonal to each other: for two different modes, the positive and negative products cancel out exactly when added up. A mode paired with itself gives \(\langle X_n, X_n \rangle = L/2\).
For those familiar with linear algebra, this is the dot product \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_i u_i v_i\), applied to functions. As an exercise, you can show that the continuous functions on \([0, L]\) form a vector space, and that \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\) behaves like a dot product.



Due to this special property, if we multiply the whole sum by \(\sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right)\) and add up the result along the string, every term except the third adds up to zero:
\[
\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle = b_3 \langle X_3, X_3 \rangle
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
b_3 = \frac{\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle}{\langle X_3, X_3 \rangle} = \frac{\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle}{L/2}
\]






TipAn analogy in vector spaces.





Let \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\). They are orthonormal: \(\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_j = 0\) for \(i \neq j\), and \(\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_i = 1\). Any vector can be written as \(\mathbf{v} = v_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + v_2 \mathbf{e}_2 + v_3 \mathbf{e}_3\), where \(v_1, v_2, v_3\) are the scalar multiples.
We can recover \(v_2\) by taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{e}_2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{e}_2 &= v_1 (\mathbf{e}_1 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_2 (\mathbf{e}_2 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_3 (\mathbf{e}_3 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) \\
                              &= v_1 (0) + v_2 (1) + v_3 (0) = v_2
\end{aligned}
\]



The same trick works for every mode, so we can find each \(b_n\) one at a time:
\[
b_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L \varphi(x)\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx
\]
Solving the integral numerically, we can now find out what are the different modes that contribute to our triangle.
