text:
Simulating the harmonics
Here are the first 16 mode for a string plucked a quarter of the way along, each scaled by its \(b_n\). The black line is the triangle we want to build:





The first 16 mode for a string plucked at 0.25, each scaled by its \(b_n\). The black line is the triangle.




The fundamental, the blue hump, is the largest, but it peaks in the middle of the string, not at the pluck point. This where the other modes, or harmonics come into play.
The 2nd mode, in orange, is much smaller. It is positive on the left half and negative on the right, so it pushes the shape up near the pluck point and down on the far side. The third mode is smaller again, and the higher harmonics shrink quickly. By the 16th they are barely visible.
Now let see what happens if we add the modes one at a time. Every curve below adds one more mode to the curve before it. We should see that it starts converging into a triangle shape.





Each curve adds one more mode to the curve before it. The black line is the exact triangle.




The fundamental alone is a poor match for the triangle, but adding the 2nd mode pulls the peak towards the pluck point. Every mode after that makes a smaller adjustment, which slowly pulls the string to the side of the triangle.
The last part to form is the corner. Even with 16 modes, the peak is still slightly rounded. Whereas the smooth sides of the triangle need only a few modes, the sharp corner needs many high modes working together. This was the heart of Euler and d’Alembert’s objection: no finite number of smooth sine waves can ever make a perfectly sharp corner.
But \(b_n\) also depend on where the string is plucked. Change where you pluck and you change how much of each mode contributes to the triangle.





Adding modes 1 to 16 for three pluck points. Plucked in the middle, the curves settle almost immediately. Plucked near the end, many high modes are needed before the sharp corner forms.




You can try this right now at your guitar!
Pluck an open string right next to the bridge and you get a harsh, pinched, twangy “eeee”. The reason being that pluck point excites lots of high harmonics as the sharp corner is at the end of the string, just like the bottom panel shows. The fundamental carries a smaller share of the shape, and the higher harmonics carry much more, which together forms harshness.
Now pluck the same string over the 12th fret, exactly halfway along. As every even harmonics has a note at the middle of the string, there is barely any even harmonics. The sound is dominated by the fundamental with little odds harmonics, and the curves settle onto the triangle almost immediately: this leads to a softer, rounder, hollow sound.
But let’s take Fourier’s advice to heart and take the sum to infinity. While we cannot compute the sum to infinite modes, we can compute it until a large enough value:





Adding 100, 1,000 and 10,000 modes for three pluck points. At original size the curves are indistinguishable from the triangle; Right side shows the triangle corner zoomed (25x).




All it takes is just 10,000 modes and we are pretty much exact.
At full size, the three curves are indistinguishable from the triangle. The only place they differ is the corner, so the panels on the right zoom in on it. With 100 modes the corner is still visibly rounded. With 1,000, there is only a small ripple . With 10,000 the curve is essentially indistinguishible.
So that settles the old argument. Euler and d’Alembert were right that no finite number of smooth sine waves can make a perfectly sharp corner. But Fourier was right too: we just need an infinite amount of them.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
What even is infinite modes?
Now I hear you ask: Are there really infinite modes in real life? Does infinity even exist and what even is that???
For existence of infinity, I recommend you to consult your nearest philosophy professor. But I can answer the first question.






WarningBeware. Heavy maths.






Short answer: No, but for our ears it is good enough. Here’s the long answer:
Our Fourier model treats the string as a continuum: matter fills space smoothly, infinitely divisible so we describe it with densities. For example, the mass of a piece of string between \(a\) and \(b\) is described as a mass density function:
\[
m_{[a,b]} = \int_{a}^{b} \mu(x)\,dx
\]
Every point \(x\) along a continuum can move on its own, so the string has infinitely many degrees of freedom, and therefore infinitely many modes.
But these are just idealizations. A real string, however, is really atoms held together by electromagnetic forces.
As a first approximation though, we can model it as a chain of atoms of mass \(M\), joined by massless springs with spring constant \(\lambda\), with both ends fixed. Each moving atom is one degree of freedom, so a chain of atoms has exactly as many modes as it has moving atoms. If \(N\) is the number of spacings between atoms, the frequency of mode \(m\) is:
\[
\omega_m = 2\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{m\pi}{2N}\right), \qquad m = 1, 2, \dots, N-1 .
\]
If we suppose \(N\) to be some unimaginably big number, then for \(m \ll N\), the chain is essentially smooth and under small-angle approximation, we have \(\sin(\theta) \approx \theta\), so
\[
\omega_m \approx 2\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}} \cdot \frac{m\pi}{2N} = m \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\pi}{N}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}}}_{\omega_1} = m \cdot \omega_1
\]
and we recover the harmonic series \(f_m = mf_1\). Only when \(m\) gets close enough to \(N\) and the wavelength shrinks to just a few atoms, does the error become non-negligible.
So how close is “close enough”?
Take a 65 cm guitar string and assume that it is perfectly elastic. Its atoms are about 0.25 nm apart, so \(N \approx 2.6 \times 10^9\). As the number of atoms determine the number of modes, the string only has a few billion modes.
In the best case, human hearing reaches about 20,000 Hz, so the highest harmonic you can hear on a 110 Hz string is at around \(m = 181\). For that mode, \(\theta \approx 1.09 \times 10^{-7}\). Expanding \(\sin\theta\) as a Taylor series and taking its third order expansion, the relative error between the chain and the harmonic approximation is:
\[
\epsilon = \frac{\theta^2}{6} \approx 2.0 \times 10*^{-15}
\]
When we treat the string as a continuum by taking the harmonic approximation, the error in the audible range is right to 15 decimal places. The error only starts to stack up when we push far into inaudible territory like 1,000 modes or 10,000 modes.
So yea, infinite mode is a fiction, but it’s an extraordinarily good one.






NoteI can’t help it baby. Here’s a probability detour.





For those with experience in probabilistic measure theory, the mass density function is within the same family of functions as the probability density function:
\[
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx
\]
where \(f(x)\) is the density of a probability measure on the Borel sets of \(\mathbb{R}\), and \(\mu(x)\) is the density of a mass measure on the Borel sets of the string, \([0, L]\).
The only difference is in normalization. A mass density integrates to \(M\), while a probability density integrates to 1. Interestingly, if we divide the mass density by \(M\), we recover a pdf:
\[
f(x) = \frac{\mu(x)}{M}
\]
which is the distribution of where a random bit of string’s mass might be located in.
Under this translation, it allows us to reinterpret key physical concepts with familiar statistics:

Center of mass as mean \[
x_{cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int x\mu(x)\,dx = \mathbb{E}[X]
\]
Moment of inertia about the center of mass as variance

\[
I = \int (x-x_{cm})^2\mu(x)\,dx = $M$Var(X)
\]
As an exercise, you can show that mass is a measure.
Let \(\mu : [0, L] \to [0, \infty)\) be a continuous mass density, and for each Borel set \(B \subseteq [0, L]\) define \[
m(B) = \int_B \mu(x)\,dx
\]

Show that \(\mu\) is Borel-measurable.
Using (a), show that \(m\) is a measure on the Borel sets by verifying the measure axioms, i.e. that \(m(\varnothing) = 0\), \(m(B) \ge 0\), and \[
m\Big(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} B_i\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} m(B_i)
\] for pairwise disjoint Borel sets \(B_1, B_2,\dots\)

End of detour.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Pluck the open A string on a guitar, and a tuner will tell you it’s 110 Hz, meaning the string swings up and down 110 times every second. This count is called the frequency.
But run the same sound through a spectrum analyzer, a tool that splits a sound into its separate frequencies, and it turns out that a single note contains several frequencies at once: not just 110 Hz, but 220, 330 Hz, and so on.
Here is a recording of an open A string, plucked three times. Its fundamental \(f_1\) is 110 Hz, so we expect energy at \(f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, 4f_1, \ldots\), or at 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz and so on respectively.

The lowest of these, 110 Hz, is the fundamental, and it sets the pitch you hear. The rest, at whole-number multiples of it, are the harmonics, and are colors that set instruments apart.

We will start with the first question, as its answer will be helpful for the second question.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
A rope example
Before tackling harmonics head on, it may be helpful to think of a guitar string as a rope tied to a post, with you holding the other end and shaking it.
If you shake it at just the right rhythm, the whole rope swings as one big loop. Shake twice as often and it snaps into two loops, with a point in the middle that stays still. Three times as often gives three loops. At any rates in between, no clean pattern builds up and the rope just jiggles. How often you shake is a frequency, and these special frequencies are exactly the fundamental and its harmonics.
In physics, these patterns are called modes, and the points that never move, including the two ends, are called nodes. An up-loop followed by a down-loop makes one full wave, and its length is called the wavelength \(\lambda\). So one loop is half a wavelength.
The figure below shows each mode as a snapshot. In reality, each loop keeps flipping between up and down, while the dots stay perfectly still.





The first four modes of a string with a fundamental \(f_1\) of 110 Hz. The dots are nodes, and \(n\) is the number of loops. Each color marks one full wavelength, so at \(n = 1\) the string holds only half a wavelength.










NoteWatch this for a visual demonstration.









Notice that the frequencies in the graph, 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz, are all multiples of 110. So then, why specifically multiples?
Suppose the string has length \(L\). Both ends are held fixed on the resting line, the straight line the string lies along when it’s still, so the wave pattern has to start and end on the ends.
Starting from the resting line at the left end, the pattern only returns to it at the end of each loop. If the string’s length ended partway through a loop, the right end would be sitting above or below the line, which is physically impossible, as the ends are fixed.





Top: a pattern with 2 loops starts and ends on the resting line, so it fits the string. Bottom: a pattern with 2.5 loops ends at a peak, leaving the right end displaced (arrow).




So a mode must contain a whole number of loops. To write this as a formula, recall that one loop is half a wavelength. A mode with \(n\) loops therefore fills the string when:
\[
L = n \cdot \frac{\lambda}{2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\lambda = \frac{2L}{n}
\]
Even though the loops seem to stay in place, each pattern is really made of ripples running back and forth along the string, bouncing off the fixed ends. These ripples travel at one fixed speed \(v\), determined by the string’s tightness and weight.
For any wave, frequency is speed divided by wavelength: the faster the wave moves, or the shorter it is, the more times it vibrates each second. For mode \(n\), whose wavelength is \(\lambda_n = 2L/n\):
\[
f_n = \frac{v}{\lambda_n} = \frac{v}{2L/n} = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n f_1,
\qquad\text{where } f_1 = \frac{v}{2L}.
\]
The speed \(v\) and the length \(L\) are fixed by the string, so only \(n\) changes from mode to mode. For an ideal string, mode 2 therefore vibrates at exactly twice the frequency of mode 1, mode 3 at three times, and so on. (Real strings are slightly stiff, which nudges the higher harmonics a bit higher in frequency.) For our 110 Hz string, that gives 110, 220, 330 Hz.
This is also why turning a tuning peg changes the pitch: tightening the string makes waves travel faster, which raises \(v\), and with it every \(f_n\).
That settles the first question: a string can only vibrate cleanly at \(f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \ldots\). But in the rope example we only saw these patterns one at a time, each at a rhythm we chose. When we pluck a string, all these modes appear at the same time, each at a different strength. So what’s happening?

\begin{cases}
\dfrac{h\,x}{p}, & 0 \le x \le p \\[1.5ex]
\dfrac{h\,(L - x)}{L - p}, & p < x \le L
\end{cases}
\]
Recall that each mode is a sine wave with \(n\) loops. The starting shape can be described as below:
\[
X_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
\]






NoteDerivation of the shape formula:





Transcribing to Latex will take forever.



In the 1750s, Daniel Bernoulli proposed that the motion of a string fixed at both ends is a sum of its modes. Not everyone was convinced, and Leonhard Euler and Jean d’Alembert certainly weren’t.
D’Alembert doubted that a corner was even allowed, since the equation for a vibrating string needs the string to be smoothly curved everywhere. Euler was happy to allow corners, after all, strings are plucked and harmonics are heard, but he couldn’t see how smooth sine waves could ever add up to one discontinued corners. If a finite sum of sines is smooth, then how can an infinite sum suddenly turn non-smooth? [1]
In the early 1800s, while studying how temperature changes over time inside a solid body, Joseph Fourier made an even bolder claim. He proposed that any shape can be written as a sum of sines, including our triangle. Mathematicians now call this a Fourier series. \[
\text{triangle}(x) = b_1 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) + b_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + b_3 \sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right) + \cdots = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
\]
Each \(b_n\) describes how much of mode \(n\) is in the triangle. In our case, we would like to find the different modes that together construct our triangle.
To find one of them, say \(b_3\), we need to isolate the third mode from all the others. We do this by exploiting a property of modes called orthogonality.






TipWhat is orthogonality?





Take two functions \(f\) and \(g\) on the string, \(0 \le x \le L\). Multiply their values at each point along the string, then add up all the results. This gives a single number, called the inner product \(\langle f, g \rangle\), defined as the integral \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^L f(x)\,g(x)\,dx\). If \(\langle f, g \rangle = 0\), we say \(f\) and \(g\) are orthogonal.
The modes are orthogonal to each other: for two different modes, the positive and negative products cancel out exactly when added up. A mode paired with itself gives \(\langle X_n, X_n \rangle = L/2\).
For those familiar with linear algebra, this is the dot product \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_i u_i v_i\), applied to functions. As an exercise, you can show that the continuous functions on \([0, L]\) form a vector space, and that \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\) behaves like a dot product.



Due to this special property, if we multiply the whole sum by \(\sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right)\) and add up the result along the string, every term except the third adds up to zero:
\[
\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle = b_3 \langle X_3, X_3 \rangle
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
b_3 = \frac{\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle}{\langle X_3, X_3 \rangle} = \frac{\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle}{L/2}
\]






TipAn analogy in vector spaces.





Let \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\). They are orthonormal: \(\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_j = 0\) for \(i \neq j\), and \(\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_i = 1\). Any vector can be written as \(\mathbf{v} = v_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + v_2 \mathbf{e}_2 + v_3 \mathbf{e}_3\), where \(v_1, v_2, v_3\) are the scalar multiples.
We can recover \(v_2\) by taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{e}_2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{e}_2 &= v_1 (\mathbf{e}_1 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_2 (\mathbf{e}_2 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_3 (\mathbf{e}_3 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) \\
                              &= v_1 (0) + v_2 (1) + v_3 (0) = v_2
\end{aligned}
\]



The same trick works for every mode, so we can find each \(b_n\) one at a time:
\[
b_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L \varphi(x)\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx
\]
Solving the integral numerically, we can now find out what are the different modes that contribute to our triangle.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Simulating the harmonics
Here are the first 16 mode for a string plucked a quarter of the way along, each scaled by its \(b_n\). The black line is the triangle we want to build:





The first 16 mode for a string plucked at 0.25, each scaled by its \(b_n\). The black line is the triangle.




The fundamental, the blue hump, is the largest, but it peaks in the middle of the string, not at the pluck point. This where the other modes, or harmonics come into play.
The 2nd mode, in orange, is much smaller. It is positive on the left half and negative on the right, so it pushes the shape up near the pluck point and down on the far side. The third mode is smaller again, and the higher harmonics shrink quickly. By the 16th they are barely visible.
Now let see what happens if we add the modes one at a time. Every curve below adds one more mode to the curve before it. We should see that it starts converging into a triangle shape.





Each curve adds one more mode to the curve before it. The black line is the exact triangle.




The fundamental alone is a poor match for the triangle, but adding the 2nd mode pulls the peak towards the pluck point. Every mode after that makes a smaller adjustment, which slowly pulls the string to the side of the triangle.
The last part to form is the corner. Even with 16 modes, the peak is still slightly rounded. Whereas the smooth sides of the triangle need only a few modes, the sharp corner needs many high modes working together. This was the heart of Euler and d’Alembert’s objection: no finite number of smooth sine waves can ever make a perfectly sharp corner.
But \(b_n\) also depend on where the string is plucked. Change where you pluck and you change how much of each mode contributes to the triangle.





Adding modes 1 to 16 for three pluck points. Plucked in the middle, the curves settle almost immediately. Plucked near the end, many high modes are needed before the sharp corner forms.




You can try this right now at your guitar!
Pluck an open string right next to the bridge and you get a harsh, pinched, twangy “eeee”. The reason being that pluck point excites lots of high harmonics as the sharp corner is at the end of the string, just like the bottom panel shows. The fundamental carries a smaller share of the shape, and the higher harmonics carry much more, which together forms harshness.
Now pluck the same string over the 12th fret, exactly halfway along. As every even harmonics has a note at the middle of the string, there is barely any even harmonics. The sound is dominated by the fundamental with little odds harmonics, and the curves settle onto the triangle almost immediately: this leads to a softer, rounder, hollow sound.
But let’s take Fourier’s advice to heart and take the sum to infinity. While we cannot compute the sum to infinite modes, we can compute it until a large enough value:





Adding 100, 1,000 and 10,000 modes for three pluck points. At original size the curves are indistinguishable from the triangle; Right side shows the triangle corner zoomed (25x).




All it takes is just 10,000 modes and we are pretty much exact.
At full size, the three curves are indistinguishable from the triangle. The only place they differ is the corner, so the panels on the right zoom in on it. With 100 modes the corner is still visibly rounded. With 1,000, there is only a small ripple . With 10,000 the curve is essentially indistinguishible.
So that settles the old argument. Euler and d’Alembert were right that no finite number of smooth sine waves can make a perfectly sharp corner. But Fourier was right too: we just need an infinite amount of them.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
What even is infinite modes?
Now I hear you ask: Are there really infinite modes in real life? Does infinity even exist and what even is that???
For existence of infinity, I recommend you to consult your nearest philosophy professor. But I can answer the first question.






WarningBeware. Heavy maths.






Short answer: No, but for our ears it is good enough. Here’s the long answer:
Our Fourier model treats the string as a continuum: matter fills space smoothly, infinitely divisible so we describe it with densities. For example, the mass of a piece of string between \(a\) and \(b\) is described as a mass density function:
\[
m_{[a,b]} = \int_{a}^{b} \mu(x)\,dx
\]
Every point \(x\) along a continuum can move on its own, so the string has infinitely many degrees of freedom, and therefore infinitely many modes.
But these are just idealizations. A real string, however, is really atoms held together by electromagnetic forces.
As a first approximation though, we can model it as a chain of atoms of mass \(M\), joined by massless springs with spring constant \(\lambda\), with both ends fixed. Each moving atom is one degree of freedom, so a chain of atoms has exactly as many modes as it has moving atoms. If \(N\) is the number of spacings between atoms, the frequency of mode \(m\) is:
\[
\omega_m = 2\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{m\pi}{2N}\right), \qquad m = 1, 2, \dots, N-1 .
\]
If we suppose \(N\) to be some unimaginably big number, then for \(m \ll N\), the chain is essentially smooth and under small-angle approximation, we have \(\sin(\theta) \approx \theta\), so
\[
\omega_m \approx 2\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}} \cdot \frac{m\pi}{2N} = m \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\pi}{N}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}}}_{\omega_1} = m \cdot \omega_1
\]
and we recover the harmonic series \(f_m = mf_1\). Only when \(m\) gets close enough to \(N\) and the wavelength shrinks to just a few atoms, does the error become non-negligible.
So how close is “close enough”?
Take a 65 cm guitar string and assume that it is perfectly elastic. Its atoms are about 0.25 nm apart, so \(N \approx 2.6 \times 10^9\). As the number of atoms determine the number of modes, the string only has a few billion modes.
In the best case, human hearing reaches about 20,000 Hz, so the highest harmonic you can hear on a 110 Hz string is at around \(m = 181\). For that mode, \(\theta \approx 1.09 \times 10^{-7}\). Expanding \(\sin\theta\) as a Taylor series and taking its third order expansion, the relative error between the chain and the harmonic approximation is:
\[
\epsilon = \frac{\theta^2}{6} \approx 2.0 \times 10*^{-15}
\]
When we treat the string as a continuum by taking the harmonic approximation, the error in the audible range is right to 15 decimal places. The error only starts to stack up when we push far into inaudible territory like 1,000 modes or 10,000 modes.
So yea, infinite mode is a fiction, but it’s an extraordinarily good one.






NoteI can’t help it baby. Here’s a probability detour.





For those with experience in probabilistic measure theory, the mass density function is within the same family of functions as the probability density function:
\[
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx
\]
where \(f(x)\) is the density of a probability measure on the Borel sets of \(\mathbb{R}\), and \(\mu(x)\) is the density of a mass measure on the Borel sets of the string, \([0, L]\).
The only difference is in normalization. A mass density integrates to \(M\), while a probability density integrates to 1. Interestingly, if we divide the mass density by \(M\), we recover a pdf:
\[
f(x) = \frac{\mu(x)}{M}
\]
which is the distribution of where a random bit of string’s mass might be located in.
Under this translation, it allows us to reinterpret key physical concepts with familiar statistics:

Center of mass as mean \[
x_{cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int x\mu(x)\,dx = \mathbb{E}[X]
\]
Moment of inertia about the center of mass as variance

\[
I = \int (x-x_{cm})^2\mu(x)\,dx = $M$Var(X)
\]
As an exercise, you can show that mass is a measure.
Let \(\mu : [0, L] \to [0, \infty)\) be a continuous mass density, and for each Borel set \(B \subseteq [0, L]\) define \[
m(B) = \int_B \mu(x)\,dx
\]

Show that \(\mu\) is Borel-measurable.
Using (a), show that \(m\) is a measure on the Borel sets by verifying the measure axioms, i.e. that \(m(\varnothing) = 0\), \(m(B) \ge 0\), and \[
m\Big(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} B_i\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} m(B_i)
\] for pairwise disjoint Borel sets \(B_1, B_2,\dots\)

End of detour.

This is why a plucked string sounds the way it does. The string doesn’t sound one frequency, but it sounds all of its harmonics at once: 110, 220, 330 Hz and up. The fundamental sets the pitch you hear, and the mix of the others, decided by where and how the string is plucked, sets its colour.

title: On Piano Tuning.
text:
Press any C on a piano, then count the keys before you reach the next one. Twelve notes: seven white keys, five black. I’ve played this layout for decades, and only recently did it strike me as strange. Why twelve? Why not ten, fifteen or even fifty-three (wink)?
The easy answer is convenience. A few more notes per octave would add around twenty keys (the horror). But convenience explains why we don’t have fifty-three notes per octave; but not why don’t we do ten, or seven, which would be even easier. And tuning systems with 19, 24, even 31 notes per octave exist, just glance at Wikipedia [1] on this topic. So, again: why twelve?
My suspicion is that the magic number comes from something deeper: hidden within the arithmetic of musical intervals. This article document my journey of discovering this truth. Beware: there will be mathematics.

text:
The Physics of Pitches
We must first start by introducing the fundamental unit of music - a note. Physically, a note is just air pressure wobbling back and forth. What sets apart notes are its pitches, measured in frequency.






NoteWhat are frequencies?





Frequency is how many times something repeats each second. A vibrating string swings back and forth, and one full back-and-forth is a cycle. The number of cycles per second is measured in hertz (Hz). A 3 Hz wave completes 3 cycles every second, and a 6 Hz wave completes 6, so it repeats twice as fast.





Two waves over one second. The lower one has twice the frequency.




For sound, frequency is pitch: more cycles per second sounds higher. The A string’s 110 Hz means it swings back and forth 110 times every second.



But a note is never one frequency. If you pluck the open A string on a guitar, a tuner will tell you it’s 110 Hz. But run the same sound through a spectrum analyzer, and odds are you will be surprised. It turns out that there are multiple frequencies in a note, not just 110 Hz, but 220, 330 Hz, and so on. The lowest of these, 110 Hz, is the fundamental, and it sets the pitch you hear. The rest, at whole-number multiples of it, are the harmonics, or overtones.
Here is a recording of an open A string, plucked three times. Its fundamental \(f_0\) is 110 Hz, so we expect energy at \(f_0, 2f_0, 3f_0, 4f_0, \ldots\), or at 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz and so on respectively.



                
                    
                    Your browser does not support the audio element.
                
              


A spectrogram shows which frequencies are present at each moment, and brighter indicates higher energy. The dashed lines mark where the theoretical harmonics should be:





Spectrogram of the recorded A string. Dashed lines mark the fundamental \(f_0\) and harmonics \(f_n = n f_0\).




Two things stand out:

The bands sit on the dashed lines. Energy is concentrated at whole-number multiples of 110 Hz, just as predicted.






NoteReal strings are not perfectly elastic!





Real harmonics roughly follow \(f_n \approx n \cdot f_0 \cdot \sqrt{1 + B n^2}\), where \(B\) is the inharmonicity coefficient. Dashed lines may not be perfectly alligned with the peaks.



Higher harmonics are weaker and shorter-lived. Most of the energy sits below about 1000 Hz, and the upper bands fade within a second or so while the low ones ring on.

For why harmonics exist, see my writing on the physics of harmonics in On Harmonics.
